docs.title: Implementation approach
docs.text:
Everything lives in one script, code/perceptron.py, written with NumPy and Matplotlib only. It generates both datasets, trains the perceptron, saves Figures 1 to 6 to figures/, and writes every number quoted below to code/results.json. To reproduce from the repository root:

pip install -r requirements.txt
python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/perceptron.py

Design choices:

  • One generator. rng = np.random.default_rng(42) is created once at the top and used, in this order, for: Exercise 1 data, the Exercise 1 initial weights, Exercise 2 data, the Exercise 2 initial weights. Nothing else draws random numbers, so the numbers below are identical on every run.
  • Shuffling. After the 1000 + 1000 points are drawn, the rows are permuted once (with the same rng). Without this the online loop would see all of Class 0 and then all of Class 1, which only changes the order of updates, but makes the run depend on an arbitrary stacking order.
  • One training function. train_perceptron implements the activation, the prediction, the {0,1} error-driven rule and the stopping condition. Exercise 2 calls the same function unchanged; the pocket bookkeeping (a full-dataset accuracy check after each update, and a copy of (w, b) when it improves) is inside it and is harmless on separable data, where the pocket simply ends equal to the final weights.
  • Same initialization for the η = 1.0 re-run. w is drawn once from rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2) and the same vector is passed to both Exercise 1 runs, so η is really the only thing that changes.

Challenges: the pocket check evaluates the whole dataset after every update (about 78 000 updates in Exercise 2), which is the slowest part, but the script still runs in about 10 s. Figure 3 includes an epoch-0 point (accuracy of the initial weights) because Exercise 1 converges so fast that a curve starting at epoch 1 would be flat.

Code (pulled from the file that was run):

"""
Perceptron from scratch (NumPy only) -- Insper ANN-DL 2026.2, Exercise 2.

Run from the repository root:
    python docs/exercises/perceptron/code/perceptron.py

It generates both datasets, trains the perceptron, prints every number the
report quotes, saves Figures 1-6 to ../figures/ and writes results.json.
A single generator, rng = np.random.default_rng(42), is used for everything,
so every run produces exactly the same numbers and figures.
"""

import json
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import matplotlib

matplotlib.use("Agg")  # no display needed, we only save PNGs
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

HERE = Path(__file__).resolve().parent
FIG_DIR = HERE.parent / "figures"
FIG_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)

# The ONLY random generator in the whole script.
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

ETA = 0.01          # learning rate from the statement
MAX_EPOCHS = 100    # epoch cap from the statement
N_PER_CLASS = 1000  # samples per class


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Data generation
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def make_dataset(mean0, cov0, mean1, cov1, n=N_PER_CLASS):
    """Draw n points per class from two 2D Gaussians and shuffle them.

    Class 0 gets label 0 and class 1 gets label 1. The rows are shuffled once
    (with the same rng) so the training loop does not see all class-0 points
    first and then all class-1 points.
    """
    x0 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean0, cov0, size=n)
    x1 = rng.multivariate_normal(mean1, cov1, size=n)
    X = np.vstack([x0, x1])
    y = np.concatenate([np.zeros(n, dtype=int), np.ones(n, dtype=int)])
    order = rng.permutation(len(y))
    return X[order], y[order]


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# The perceptron (activation, prediction, update rule, training loop)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def step(z):
    """Heaviside activation: 1 if z >= 0, else 0."""
    return (z >= 0).astype(int)


def predict(X, w, b):
    """y_hat = step(w . x + b) for every row of X."""
    return step(X @ w + b)


def accuracy(X, y, w, b):
    """Fraction of points of the full dataset classified correctly."""
    return float(np.mean(predict(X, w, b) == y))


def train_perceptron(X, y, w0, b0=0.0, eta=ETA, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS):
    """Online perceptron with the {0,1} error-driven rule and a pocket.

    For each sample (x, y):
        y_hat = step(w . x + b)
        w <- w + eta * (y - y_hat) * x
        b <- b + eta * (y - y_hat)
    (y - y_hat) is 0 on a correct prediction, so only mistakes update.

    Stops after an epoch with zero updates, or after max_epochs.

    Pocket: after every update the accuracy on the full dataset is computed;
    if it beats the best seen so far, (w, b) is copied into the pocket.
    On separable data the pocket simply ends equal to the final weights.
    """
    w = np.array(w0, dtype=float).copy()
    b = float(b0)

    # Pocket starts with the initial weights.
    pocket_w, pocket_b = w.copy(), b
    pocket_acc = accuracy(X, y, w, b)
    pocket_epoch = 0

    history = {"acc": [], "pocket_acc": [], "updates": []}
    converged = False

    for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
        n_updates = 0
        for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
            y_hat = 1 if (xi @ w + b) >= 0 else 0  # same rule as step()
            error = yi - y_hat                    # 0, +1 or -1
            if error != 0:
                w += eta * error * xi
                b += eta * error
                n_updates += 1
                # Pocket bookkeeping: the only addition to the loop.
                acc_now = accuracy(X, y, w, b)
                if acc_now > pocket_acc:
                    pocket_w, pocket_b = w.copy(), b
                    pocket_acc = acc_now
                    pocket_epoch = epoch

        history["acc"].append(accuracy(X, y, w, b))
        history["pocket_acc"].append(pocket_acc)
        history["updates"].append(n_updates)

        if n_updates == 0:  # a full clean pass: converged
            converged = True
            break

    return {
        "w": w, "b": b, "acc": accuracy(X, y, w, b),
        "epochs": epoch, "converged": converged,
        "pocket_w": pocket_w, "pocket_b": pocket_b,
        "pocket_acc": pocket_acc, "pocket_epoch": pocket_epoch,
        "history": history,
    }


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Plotting helpers (every plot: title, axis labels, class legend)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
COLORS = {0: "#1f77b4", 1: "#ff7f0e"}


def scatter_classes(ax, X, y):
    for c in (0, 1):
        m = y == c
        ax.scatter(X[m, 0], X[m, 1], s=8, alpha=0.5, c=COLORS[c],
                   label=f"Class {c}")
    ax.set_xlabel("$x_1$")
    ax.set_ylabel("$x_2$")


def draw_boundary(ax, w, b, X, **kw):
    """Draw w1*x1 + w2*x2 + b = 0 across the x-range of the data."""
    x1 = np.linspace(X[:, 0].min() - 1, X[:, 0].max() + 1, 200)
    if abs(w[1]) > 1e-12:
        ax.plot(x1, -(w[0] * x1 + b) / w[1], **kw)
    else:  # vertical line
        ax.axvline(-b / w[0], **kw)


def mark_errors(ax, X, y, w, b, marker="x", color="red", label="Misclassified"):
    wrong = predict(X, w, b) != y
    if wrong.any():
        ax.scatter(X[wrong, 0], X[wrong, 1], marker=marker, s=30,
                   c=color, linewidths=1, label=f"{label} ({wrong.sum()})")
    return int(wrong.sum())


def save(fig, name):
    fig.tight_layout()
    fig.savefig(FIG_DIR / name, dpi=150)
    plt.close(fig)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exercise 1 -- separable data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X1, y1 = make_dataset([1.5, 1.5], [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]],
                      [5.0, 5.0], [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
scatter_classes(ax, X1, y1)
ax.set_title("Figure 1 - Exercise 1: separable data (2000 points)")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig1.png")

# Initialization: w ~ N(0, 0.01), b = 0. Drawn ONCE and reused for the
# eta = 1.0 re-run, so that eta is the only thing that changes.
w_init_1 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)

r1 = train_perceptron(X1, y1, w_init_1, eta=0.01)
r1_eta1 = train_perceptron(X1, y1, w_init_1, eta=1.0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
scatter_classes(ax, X1, y1)
draw_boundary(ax, r1["w"], r1["b"], X1, color="black", lw=2,
              label="Decision boundary ($\\eta$=0.01)")
n_err_1 = mark_errors(ax, X1, y1, r1["w"], r1["b"])
ax.set_ylim(X1[:, 1].min() - 1, X1[:, 1].max() + 1)
ax.set_title("Figure 2 - Exercise 1: learned decision boundary")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
save(fig, "fig2.png")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 4))
# epoch 0 = accuracy of the initial weights, before any training
acc0_1 = accuracy(X1, y1, w_init_1, 0.0)
ax.plot(np.arange(0, r1["epochs"] + 1), [acc0_1] + r1["history"]["acc"],
        "o-", label="$\\eta$ = 0.01")
ax.plot(np.arange(0, r1_eta1["epochs"] + 1), [acc0_1] + r1_eta1["history"]["acc"],
        "s--", label="$\\eta$ = 1.0 (item D)")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(0, max(r1["epochs"], r1_eta1["epochs"]) + 1))
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy on the full dataset")
ax.set_title("Figure 3 - Exercise 1: accuracy x epoch")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
save(fig, "fig3.png")


def unit(v):
    return v / np.linalg.norm(v)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Exercise 2 -- overlapping data
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
X2, y2 = make_dataset([3.0, 3.0], [[1.5, 0], [0, 1.5]],
                      [4.0, 4.0], [[1.5, 0], [0, 1.5]])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(6, 5))
scatter_classes(ax, X2, y2)
ax.set_title("Figure 4 - Exercise 2: overlapping data (2000 points)")
ax.legend()
save(fig, "fig4.png")

w_init_2 = rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)
r2 = train_perceptron(X2, y2, w_init_2, eta=ETA)  # same function, unchanged

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 5.5))
scatter_classes(ax, X2, y2)
draw_boundary(ax, r2["w"], r2["b"], X2, color="red", lw=2, ls="--",
              label="Final boundary")
draw_boundary(ax, r2["pocket_w"], r2["pocket_b"], X2, color="black", lw=2,
              label="Pocket boundary")
mark_errors(ax, X2, y2, r2["pocket_w"], r2["pocket_b"], marker="x",
            color="black", label="Misclassified by pocket")
mark_errors(ax, X2, y2, r2["w"], r2["b"], marker="o", color="none",
            label="Misclassified by final")
# hollow red circles for the final-weight errors
for coll in ax.collections[-1:]:
    coll.set_edgecolor("red")
    coll.set_facecolor("none")
ax.set_xlim(X2[:, 0].min() - 0.5, X2[:, 0].max() + 0.5)
ax.set_ylim(X2[:, 1].min() - 0.5, X2[:, 1].max() + 0.5)
ax.set_title("Figure 5 - Exercise 2: final vs pocket boundary")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=8)
save(fig, "fig5.png")

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4))
ep2 = np.arange(1, r2["epochs"] + 1)
ax.plot(ep2, r2["history"]["acc"], lw=1, label="Current weights")
ax.plot(ep2, r2["history"]["pocket_acc"], lw=2, label="Pocket (best so far)")
ax.axhline(0.5, color="gray", ls=":", label="Chance (50%)")
ax.set_xlabel("Epoch")
ax.set_ylabel("Accuracy on the full dataset")
ax.set_title("Figure 6 - Exercise 2: accuracy x epoch")
ax.legend()
ax.grid(alpha=0.3)
save(fig, "fig6.png")

# Where does the final boundary cut the diagonal x1 = x2 = t ?
# (w1 + w2) t + b = 0  ->  t = -b / (w1 + w2)
t_final = -r2["b"] / r2["w"].sum()
t_pocket = -r2["pocket_b"] / r2["pocket_w"].sum()
pred_final = predict(X2, r2["w"], r2["b"])

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Supplementary checks quoted in the D items (they draw nothing from rng)
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Ex1 D3: from a zero start, eta only rescales the weights.
z_a = train_perceptron(X1, y1, np.zeros(2), eta=0.01)
z_b = train_perceptron(X1, y1, np.zeros(2), eta=1.0)
zero_start = {
    "epochs_eta001": z_a["epochs"], "epochs_eta1": z_b["epochs"],
    "w_ratio": (z_b["w"] / z_a["w"]).tolist(),
    "b_ratio": z_b["b"] / z_a["b"],
}

# Ex2 D1: best accuracy any straight line reaches on THIS sample.
# Sweep directions theta and, for each, every threshold along the projection.
best_line_acc = 0.0
for theta in np.linspace(0, np.pi, 721):
    d = np.array([np.cos(theta), np.sin(theta)])
    proj = X2 @ d
    order = np.argsort(proj)
    ys = y2[order]
    # predict 1 to the right of the cut: correct = (#0 left) + (#1 right)
    zeros_left = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum(ys == 0)])
    ones_right = np.concatenate([[0], np.cumsum((ys == 1)[::-1])])[::-1]
    best_line_acc = max(best_line_acc, ((zeros_left + ones_right).max()) / len(ys))

# Ex2 D3: more epochs / smaller eta (same data, same initial weights).
more_epochs = train_perceptron(X2, y2, w_init_2, eta=0.01, max_epochs=500)
small_eta = train_perceptron(X2, y2, w_init_2, eta=0.001, max_epochs=100)
supp_ex2 = {
    "best_line_acc": float(best_line_acc),
    "epochs500_final_acc": more_epochs["acc"],
    "epochs500_pocket_acc": more_epochs["pocket_acc"],
    "epochs500_last100_acc_range": [min(more_epochs["history"]["acc"][-100:]),
                                    max(more_epochs["history"]["acc"][-100:])],
    "eta0001_final_acc": small_eta["acc"],
    "eta0001_pocket_acc": small_eta["pocket_acc"],
    "eta0001_acc_range": [min(small_eta["history"]["acc"]),
                          max(small_eta["history"]["acc"])],
}

# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
# Print and save every reported number
# ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
results = {
    "ex1": {
        "w_init": w_init_1.tolist(),
        "acc_epoch0": acc0_1,
        "w": r1["w"].tolist(), "b": r1["b"], "epochs": r1["epochs"],
        "converged": r1["converged"], "acc": r1["acc"],
        "updates_per_epoch": r1["history"]["updates"],
        "acc_per_epoch": r1["history"]["acc"],
        "dir": unit(r1["w"]).tolist(),
        "misclassified": n_err_1,
    },
    "ex1_eta1": {
        "w": r1_eta1["w"].tolist(), "b": r1_eta1["b"],
        "epochs": r1_eta1["epochs"], "converged": r1_eta1["converged"],
        "acc": r1_eta1["acc"],
        "updates_per_epoch": r1_eta1["history"]["updates"],
        "dir": unit(r1_eta1["w"]).tolist(),
        "angle_deg": float(np.degrees(np.arccos(
            np.clip(unit(r1["w"]) @ unit(r1_eta1["w"]), -1, 1)))),
    },
    "ex2": {
        "w_init": w_init_2.tolist(),
        "w": r2["w"].tolist(), "b": r2["b"], "acc": r2["acc"],
        "epochs": r2["epochs"], "converged": r2["converged"],
        "pocket_w": r2["pocket_w"].tolist(), "pocket_b": r2["pocket_b"],
        "pocket_acc": r2["pocket_acc"], "pocket_epoch": r2["pocket_epoch"],
        "updates_per_epoch": r2["history"]["updates"],
        "acc_per_epoch": r2["history"]["acc"],
        "acc_min": min(r2["history"]["acc"]),
        "acc_max": max(r2["history"]["acc"]),
        "final_pred_frac_class1": float(pred_final.mean()),
        "diag_cut_final": float(t_final),
        "diag_cut_pocket": float(t_pocket),
        "mean_norm_x": float(np.linalg.norm(X2, axis=1).mean()),
    },
    "ex1_zero_start": zero_start,
    "ex2_supplementary": supp_ex2,
}

with open(HERE / "results.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(results, f, indent=2)

print(json.dumps(results, indent=2))

docs.title: A — Generate the data
docs.text:
Class 0: mean [1.5, 1.5], covariance [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]]. Class 1: mean [5, 5], covariance [[0.5, 0], [0, 0.5]]. 1000 samples per class (function make_dataset).

Figure 1. The two classes are far apart relative to their spread: there is a wide empty corridor between them.

docs.title: B — Implement the perceptron
docs.text:
• Prediction: ŷ = step(w·x + b), with step(z) = 1 if z ≥ 0 and 0 otherwise (step, predict).
  • Update, for each sample: w ← w + η(y − ŷ)x and b ← b + η(y − ŷ). The error y − ŷ is 0 on a correct prediction, +1 on a false negative and −1 on a false positive, so both kinds of mistake get corrected.
  • Initialization: w = [0.00991, −0.00827] (drawn from rng.normal(0, 0.01, size=2)), b = 0.
  • η = 0.01; stop after an epoch with zero updates or after 100 epochs; accuracy on the full dataset recorded after every epoch.

docs.title: C — Train and measure
docs.text:
• Final w = [0.03189, 0.02874], final b = −0.200.
  • Epochs: 2. Epoch 1 made 48 updates; epoch 2 made 0 updates, which is the stopping condition.
  • Final accuracy: 100.0% (0 misclassified points). The initial weights scored 61.5%.

The boundary 0.03189·x₁ + 0.02874·x₂ − 0.200 = 0 crosses the diagonal x₁ = x₂ at 3.30, inside the empty corridor between the two means (1.5 and 5).

Figure 2. Decision boundary over the data. No point is misclassified, so there are no markers.

Figure 3. Accuracy × epoch (epoch 0 = initial weights). Both learning rates reach 100% at the end of epoch 1 and stop at epoch 2.

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. Why separable data converges quickly. An update happens only when y − ŷ ≠ 0, i.e. only on a mistake. Each mistake pushes w toward the misclassified point (+x for a false negative, −x for a false positive), so the boundary moves to the correct side of it. Because a separating line exists with a large margin, the number of points the current line gets wrong can only shrink: here it went from 48 updates in epoch 1 to 0 in epoch 2. Once a full pass has no mistakes, nothing in the rule can change w or b anymore, so training stops by itself.

2. η = 1.0. Same data, same initial w, only η changed:

Run Epochs Updates (epoch 1) Accuracy w b w / ‖w‖ η = 0.01 2 48 100% [0.03189, 0.02874] −0.20 [0.7429, 0.6694] η = 1.0 2 25 100% [1.71734, 1.66459] −11.0 [0.7181, 0.6960]

The two directions differ by 2.09°, and the boundaries cross the diagonal at 3.30 and 3.25: both separate the data perfectly, but they are different lines. Writing the weights after the training as w = w₀ + η Σ eᵢxᵢ (eᵢ = ±1 on the mistakes), dividing by η gives w/η = w₀/η + Σ eᵢxᵢ. The boundary only depends on w up to scale, so what matters is how big the initial vector is compared with one update. With ‖w₀‖ ≈ 0.013: for η = 0.01 the initial term w₀/η has norm ≈ 1.3, comparable to a single data point (‖x‖ between 2 and 7), so the random start still shapes which points are misclassified and in what order. For η = 1.0 the initial term is ≈ 0.013, negligible after the very first update, so the run behaves almost like a zero start. η therefore controls the relative weight of the initialization against each correction: it changes the sequence of mistakes (48 vs 25) and hence which of the many separating lines is found, not whether one is found.

3. Zero start. Let w₀ = 0, b₀ = 0 and compare two runs with η₁ and η₂ on the same data in the same order. Claim: after every step k, w_k^(2) = (η₂/η₁) w_k^(1) and b_k^(2) = (η₂/η₁) b_k^(1).

  • Step 0: both are 0, so the claim holds.
  • Inductive step: if the claim holds at step k, then for the next sample w^(2)·x + b^(2) = (η₂/η₁)(w^(1)·x + b^(1)). Since η₂/η₁ > 0, multiplying by it does not change the sign, so step(·) gives the same ŷ in both runs and the same error e = y − ŷ. The updates are η₁e·x and η₂e·x = (η₂/η₁)·η₁e·x, so after the update the claim still holds.

So both runs make exactly the same mistakes, at the same samples, in the same epochs: same epoch count, and the weights differ only by the factor η₂/η₁. The boundary {w·x + b = 0} is unchanged by scaling (w, b) by a positive constant, so η has no effect at all. Running it confirms this: from zero, η = 0.01 and η = 1.0 both stop at epoch 2, and the ratios of w₁, w₂ and b between the runs are all exactly 100.0. This is why item B forbids the zero start: with it, the η comparison in item 2 would be empty.

docs.title: A — Generate the data
docs.text:
Class 0: mean [3, 3], covariance [[1.5, 0], [0, 1.5]]. Class 1: mean [4, 4], covariance [[1.5, 0], [0, 1.5]]. 1000 samples per class, same make_dataset function and same rng.

Figure 4. The clouds overlap heavily; no straight line separates them.

docs.title: B — Train, keeping the best weights
docs.text:
Same train_perceptron, η = 0.01, 100-epoch cap, initial w = [−0.01456, −0.00462] (next draw of the same rng), b = 0. The loop never had a clean epoch: it made between roughly 750 and 820 updates in every one of the 100 epochs.

Weights w b Accuracy Final (after epoch 100) [0.06818, 0.09646] −0.460 64.85% Pocket (best so far) [0.07095, 0.06505] −0.480 70.70%

The pocket best was found during epoch 40. For reference, the best accuracy any straight line reaches on this particular sample (exhaustive sweep over directions and offsets, in the script) is 70.75%, so the pocket is essentially optimal for this draw. The ~73% in the statement is what the best line reaches in expectation; with the theoretical distributions the Bayes-optimal line x₁ + x₂ = 7 gives Φ(0.577) ≈ 72%, and a finite sample of 2000 points lands a little above or below that.

The final iterate did not drop all the way to 50% in this run; it ends at 64.85% and its per-epoch accuracy wanders between 60.8% and 68.3% (Figure 6). Item D explains why it sits below the pocket and why its value is essentially arbitrary.

docs.title: C — Figures
docs.text:
Figure 5. Final boundary (red dashed) and pocket boundary (black). Black ×: points misclassified by the pocket weights (586). Red circles: points misclassified by the final weights (703).

Figure 6. Accuracy of the current weights after each epoch (oscillates, never settles) and of the pocket weights (monotone, flat at 70.7% from epoch 40).

docs.title: D — Analysis
docs.text:
1. The gap between final and pocket. The pocket line crosses the diagonal x₁ = x₂ at 3.53, practically at the midpoint (3.5) between the two means, and its direction w/‖w‖ = [0.737, 0.676] is almost the diagonal: that is the best line. The final line crosses the diagonal at 2.79, inside the Class 0 cloud, and is tilted: it labels 75.8% of all points as Class 1, so it misclassifies a large part of Class 0 and only scores 64.85%.

The reason is in the sizes of the steps. Per mistake, b moves by η = 0.01, while w moves by η·x, whose norm is about 0.01 × 5.1 = 0.051 (mean ‖x‖ = 5.11 here). The weights themselves are only ‖w‖ ≈ 0.1, so one mistake changes w by about half of its own length, while it changes b by about 2%. The boundary's position along the diagonal is t = −b/(w₁ + w₂); a single false negative adds x₁ + x₂ ≈ 7 × 0.01 = 0.07 to w₁ + w₂ (about 40% of it) but only 0.01 to b, so the line lurches toward Class 0; a false positive does the opposite. Since every possible line misclassifies at least ~29% of the points, there are about 780 such lurches per epoch, and the boundary never stops being kicked around the overlap region. The loop leaves it "there" only because the 100-epoch cap happened to stop it after some last run of mistakes: the final weights are a snapshot of a random walk, not a solution. In a long run the snapshot can be much worse than ours (see item 3: in epochs 401 to 500 the current accuracy went as low as 54.5%, close to the ~50% the statement warns about). The pocket ignores where the walk is now and keeps the best point it ever visited.

2. Figure 3 vs Figure 6, and the convergence theorem. The perceptron convergence theorem (Novikoff, 1962) says: if there is a weight vector w* that classifies every training point correctly with a positive margin γ, and every point has ‖x‖ ≤ R, then the perceptron makes at most (R/γ)² mistakes in total, whatever the order of the samples. A finite number of mistakes means a finite number of updates, so the weights stop changing and the accuracy curve settles, which is Figure 3 (48 mistakes, then none). The assumption this dataset violates is linear separability: no w* with γ > 0 exists, because the clouds overlap. Without it the theorem gives no bound, mistakes keep happening forever (750+ per epoch), and the curve in Figure 6 keeps oscillating.

3. More epochs? Smaller η? Neither fixes it.

  • More epochs. For any (w, b), at least 29% of the points are misclassified, so every epoch triggers hundreds of updates; the rule has no state in which it stops changing. More epochs only lengthen the random walk: the final iterate stays as arbitrary as before, and the only thing that can improve is the pocket. Check (same data, same initial weights, 500 epochs): final accuracy 63.4%, current accuracy in the last 100 epochs between 54.5% and 68.3%, pocket 70.75%.
  • Smaller η. After the first few updates the initial w is negligible and w ≈ η Σ eᵢxᵢ, b ≈ η Σ eᵢ. As shown in Exercise 1 D3, multiplying η by a constant multiplies w and b by the same constant and leaves the predictions, the mistakes and the boundary unchanged. In particular the relative kick per mistake, ‖ηx‖/‖w‖, does not depend on η, because ‖w‖ itself scales with η. A smaller η gives the same walk at a smaller scale. Check: η = 0.001 for 100 epochs gives a final accuracy of 68.25% and a per-epoch range of 61.0% to 68.35%, the same band as η = 0.01; pocket 70.7%.

What actually fixes it is changing the algorithm, not its settings: keep the pocket (as done here), average the iterates, or use a loss with a decaying step size (e.g. logistic regression) instead of the mistake-driven step rule.

def train_perceptron(X, y, w0, b0=0.0, eta=ETA, max_epochs=MAX_EPOCHS):
    """Online perceptron with the {0,1} error-driven rule and a pocket.

    For each sample (x, y):
        y_hat = step(w . x + b)
        w <- w + eta * (y - y_hat) * x
        b <- b + eta * (y - y_hat)
    (y - y_hat) is 0 on a correct prediction, so only mistakes update.

    Stops after an epoch with zero updates, or after max_epochs.

    Pocket: after every update the accuracy on the full dataset is computed;
    if it beats the best seen so far, (w, b) is copied into the pocket.
    On separable data the pocket simply ends equal to the final weights.
    """
    w = np.array(w0, dtype=float).copy()
    b = float(b0)

    # Pocket starts with the initial weights.
    pocket_w, pocket_b = w.copy(), b
    pocket_acc = accuracy(X, y, w, b)
    pocket_epoch = 0

    history = {"acc": [], "pocket_acc": [], "updates": []}
    converged = False

    for epoch in range(1, max_epochs + 1):
        n_updates = 0
        for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
            y_hat = 1 if (xi @ w + b) >= 0 else 0  # same rule as step()
            error = yi - y_hat                    # 0, +1 or -1
            if error != 0:
                w += eta * error * xi
                b += eta * error
                n_updates += 1
                # Pocket bookkeeping: the only addition to the loop.
                acc_now = accuracy(X, y, w, b)
                if acc_now > pocket_acc:
                    pocket_w, pocket_b = w.copy(), b
                    pocket_acc = acc_now
                    pocket_epoch = epoch

        history["acc"].append(accuracy(X, y, w, b))
        history["pocket_acc"].append(pocket_acc)
        history["updates"].append(n_updates)

        if n_updates == 0:  # a full clean pass: converged
            converged = True
            break

    return {
        "w": w, "b": b, "acc": accuracy(X, y, w, b),
        "epochs": epoch, "converged": converged,
        "pocket_w": pocket_w, "pocket_b": pocket_b,
        "pocket_acc": pocket_acc, "pocket_epoch": pocket_epoch,
        "history": history,
    }

docs.title: Exploring Class Separability in 2D¶
docs.text: Understanding how data is distributed is the first step before designing a network architecture. In this exercise, you will generate and visualize a two-dimensional dataset to explore how data distribution affects the complexity of the decision boundaries a neural network would need to learn.

docs.title: Instructions¶
docs.text:
1. Generate the Data: Create a synthetic dataset with a total of 400 samples, divided equally among 4 classes (100 samples each). Use a Gaussian distribution to generate the points for each class based on the following parameters:
    • Class 0: Mean = [2, 3], Standard Deviation = [0.8, 2.5]
    • Class 1: Mean = [5, 6], Standard Deviation = [1.2, 1.9]
    • Class 2: Mean = [8, 1], Standard Deviation = [0.9, 0.9]
    • Class 3: Mean = [15, 4], Standard Deviation = [0.5, 2.0]

docs.title: Non-Linearity in Higher Dimensions¶
docs.text: Simple neural networks (like a Perceptron) can only learn linear boundaries. Deep networks excel when data is not linearly separable. This exercise challenges you to create and visualize such a dataset.

    • Class B:

docs.title: Preparing Real-World Data for a Neural Network¶
docs.text: This exercise uses a real dataset from Kaggle. Your task is to perform the necessary preprocessing to make it suitable for a neural network that uses the hyperbolic tangent (tanh) activation function in its hidden layers.

docs.title: Instructions¶
docs.text:
1. Get the Data: Download the Spaceship Titanic dataset from Kaggle.

  2. Describe the Data:

    • Briefly describe the dataset's objective (i.e., what does the Transported column represent?).

      • We're trying to predict if a passenger was transported to another dimension during the crash of the Spaceship Titanic, the value that represents whether or not the passenger was transported is in the Transported column

    • List the features and identify which are numerical (e.g., Age, RoomService) and which are categorical (e.g., HomePlanet, Destination).

    • Investigate the dataset for missing values. Which columns have them, and how many?

Categorical Columns -

  • HomePlanet - The planet the passenger departed from, typically their planet of permanent residence.
  • Cabin - The cabin number where the passenger is staying. Takes the form deck/num/side, where side can be either P for Port or S for Starboard.
  • Destination - The planet the passenger will be debarking to.
  • Name - The first and last names of the passenger.
  • PassengerId - A unique Id for each passenger. Each Id takes the form gggg_pp where gggg indicates a group the passenger is travelling with and pp is their number within the group. People in a group are often family members, but not always.

Boolean Columns -

  • Transported - Whether the passenger was transported to another dimension. This is the target, the column you are trying to predict.
  • VIP - Whether the passenger has paid for special VIP service during the voyage.
  • CryoSleep - Indicates whether the passenger elected to be put into suspended animation for the duration of the voyage. Passengers in cryosleep are confined to their cabins.

Numerical Columns -

  • Age - The age of the passenger.
  • RoomService, FoodCourt, ShoppingMall, Spa, VRDeck - Amount the passenger has billed at each of the Spaceship Titanic's many luxury amenities.

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
O material utiliza o mkdocs para gerar a documentação. Para visualizar a documentação, execute o comando:

mkdocs serve -o

Para subir ao GitHub Pages, execute o comando:

mkdocs gh-deploy

Esse repositório possui um workflow do GitHub Actions que executa o comando mkdocs gh-deploy sempre que houver um push na branch main. Assim, não é necessário executar esse comando manualmente. Toda vez que você fizer um push na branch main, a documentação será atualizada automaticamente no GitHub Pages.

Aviso 1

Para que o github actions funcione corretamente, é necessário que o repositório esteja configurado para que o bot github-actions[bot] tenha permissão de escrita. Você pode verificar isso nas configurações do repositório, na seção "Actions" e depois em "General". Certifique-se de que a opção "Workflow permissions" esteja definida como "Read and write permissions".

Aviso 2

Depois de publicar, caso não consiga acessar a página, verifique se o github pages está configurado corretamente. Vá até as configurações do repositório, na seção "Pages" e verifique se a branch gh-pages está selecionada como fonte. Se não estiver, selecione-a e salve as alterações.

Pay Attention

No arquivo 'mkdocs.yml, a seção site_url deve estar configurada corretamente para o seu repositório. Por exemplo, se o seu repositório estiver em https://github.com/usuario/repositorio, a seção site_url deve ser:

site_url: https://usuario.github.io/repositorio

Também, certifique-se de que a seção repo_url esteja configurada corretamente para o seu repositório. Por exemplo:

repo_url: https://github.com/usuario/repositorio
